name: Intellectual property complaint (trademark, copyright, patent), account or ASIN level

intake.label: What date is on the notice?
intake.why: The appeal opens by naming the ASINs, the complaint ID and the notice date.

intake.label: What is the complaint ID in the notice?
intake.why: Amazon cannot match a retraction to your account without it.

intake.label: Who is the rights owner named in the complaint?
intake.why: The retraction has to come from them, to Amazon, quoting the complaint ID.

intake.label: What kind of right is it?
intake.why: Each has a different defence. A trademark claim on a genuine product is often exhaustion or first sale; a copyright claim is usually about images or text you can simply change.

intake.label: Which ASINs are affected?
intake.why: The appeal addresses each ASIN in the complaint.

intake.label: Which path fits your situation?
options: The rights owner will retract, or I can ask them
I have authorisation to sell this brand
The listing was mine and in error, I have removed it
The product is genuine and I have the supply chain
intake.why: There are only these routes back. We draft the one your answers support, not all four.

intake.label: If you have authorisation, who issued it and when?
intake.why: An authorisation letter that does not name your business or is undated will not be accepted.

showIf.equals: I have authorisation to sell this brand

intake.label: If the listing was in error, what exactly was wrong with it? (image, brand name in title, description text)
intake.why: The corrective action has to name the element that infringed and the date you fixed it.

showIf.equals: The listing was mine and in error, I have removed it

intake.label: Have you contacted the rights owner? What happened?
intake.why: Amazon expects you to try. A retraction ends the case faster than any appeal.

intake.label: Who now checks brand and image rights before a listing goes live?
intake.why: Preventive measures need an owner and a cadence.

evidence.label: The infringement notice
evidence.why: We quote the complaint ID, rights owner and ASINs exactly.

evidence.label: Retraction email from the rights owner, if you have one
evidence.why: The fastest route back. Must quote the complaint ID and be sent to Amazon by the rights owner.

evidence.label: Authorisation or distributor letter naming your business
evidence.why: Evidences the right to sell the brand.

evidence.label: Supplier invoices for the affected ASINs
Your correspondence with the rights owner
evidence.why: Shows Amazon you attempted resolution at source.

sections.heading: Root cause
sections.guidance: State why the complaint arose: an image used without licence, a brand name in the title, stock sourced outside the authorised chain, or a complaint the seller believes is mistaken with the evidence that supports that.

sections.heading: Corrective actions already taken
sections.guidance: Dated bullets: listing removed or amended on a date, rights owner contacted on a date, retraction requested, stock quarantined.

sections.heading: Preventive measures
sections.guidance: Dated bullets naming the owner and the pre-listing rights check.

output.opening: One sentence naming the complaint ID, the rights owner, the ASINs and the notice date.
output.closing: One line listing the attachments by filename. Where the retraction path is chosen, a separate retraction request email to the rights owner is produced alongside the appeal.

rejection_patterns.check: The complaint ID appears in the appeal.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: Without the complaint ID Amazon cannot match your appeal to the notice.

rejection_patterns.check: The appeal does not claim authorisation unless an authorisation document is in the confirmed evidence.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: The appeal claims authorisation to sell the brand but no authorisation letter has been uploaded.

rejection_patterns.check: Every corrective and preventive bullet carries a specific date.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: A corrective action with no date reads as a promise, not an action taken.

rejection_patterns.check: No paragraph scores above 0.6 for genericity.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: This paragraph could belong to any seller. Rights teams reject template language.

rejection_patterns.check: The appeal does not argue trademark law at Amazon. It states facts and attaches documents.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: Amazon does not adjudicate infringement. Legal argument here delays the case; a retraction or an authorisation resolves it.

rejection_patterns.check: None of: unfortunately, I assure you, please give me one more chance, loyal seller, unfair.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: This phrase appears in rejected appeals more than in accepted ones. Remove it.

rejection_patterns.check: No [MISSING: ...] markers remain in the draft.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: A required fact is missing. Answer the question or upload the document.

rejection_patterns.check: The appeal says whether the rights owner has been contacted.
rejection_patterns.fail_message: The appeal does not say whether you approached the rights owner.
Over 600 words. Reviewers skim; the extra length dilutes the specifics.

submission.where: Seller Central, Account Health, Intellectual Property Complaints, or Reactivate your account for an account-level deactivation
steps: Open Seller Central and go to Performance, then Account Health.
Open the Intellectual Property Complaints tab and find the complaint ID.
Paste the appeal into the appeal box for that complaint.
Where a retraction is the chosen path, send the retraction request email to the rights owner first and ask them to email Amazon quoting the complaint ID.
Attach the authorisation letter or invoices as separate files.
submission.turnaround: Amazon's stated turnaround is 3 to 5 business days. A retraction from the rights owner is usually actioned faster.
